title: Atezolizumab 1200 mg · every 3 weeks · lung cancer
purpose: In advanced cancer the aim is cancer control and symptom relief; after surgery the aim is to reduce recurrence risk. Confirm your exact treatment setting.
context_label: Lung settings: previously treated NSCLC; first-line PD-L1-high metastatic NSCLC; adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy; ES-SCLC maintenance after induction.
indication_text: First-line metastatic NSCLC requires PD-L1 ≥50% tumour cells or ≥10% immune cells and no EGFR/ALK alteration. After prior chemotherapy, NSCLC has separate eligibility. Adjuvant use requires completely resected high-risk stage II–IIIA AJCC7, predominantly non-squamous cancer, PD-L1 ≥50%, no EGFR/ALK alteration and prior platinum chemotherapy. ES-SCLC use is maintenance after completed combination induction.
schedule_summary: Atezolizumab 1200 mg is given by intravenous infusion on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The first infusion lasts about 60 minutes; later infusions may last 30 minutes if tolerated. The visit includes checks and preparation. This protocol also offers a separately prescribed 1875 mg injection under the skin of the thigh over about 7 minutes every 3 weeks. The IV and under-skin doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram. Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.
administration_text: Atezolizumab 1200 mg is given by intravenous infusion on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). This protocol also offers a separately prescribed 1875 mg injection under the skin of the thigh over about 7 minutes every 3 weeks. monitoring_summary: Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 3-week treatment cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks; other hormones when clinically indicated. Symptoms need review during and after treatment.

agents.name: Atezolizumab
agents.mechanism: Blocks PD-L1 to support immune attack
agents.explanation: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.
agents.watch: Report new breathing, bowel, skin, hormone, heart or nerve symptoms promptly; these may be immune inflammation.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, hormone glands, skin, heart and nervous system
Some effects need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement
Effects may start after the final dose

urgent_extra: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.
consent_support: Discuss the aim for your exact lung setting, likely benefit, alternatives, important immune risks and how treatment may be paused or stopped. Some side effects need long-term medicines. Ask about fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and effects on daily life.
safety_note: Immune effects can happen on any day and after treatment ends. Carry your immunotherapy alert card and tell any healthcare team that you receive atezolizumab.

day_groups.title: Your infusion visit
day_groups.body: The team reviews your blood results, symptoms and medicines. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, a tight chest, dizziness or feeling suddenly unwell during the drip.
day_groups.action: Before leaving, confirm the next tests, treatment visit and urgent contact number.

day_groups.title: Between visits
day_groups.body: You may feel well between infusions, but immune inflammation can begin at any time. Keep a short symptom record and take medicines exactly as prescribed. Contact your team about new symptoms instead of waiting for your next appointment.
day_groups.action: Confirm thyroid checks every 3–6 weeks independently of infusion appointments.

support.title: Sickness medicines
support.text: Atezolizumab alone has a minimal risk of causing sickness. Routine anti-sickness medicines or infusion premedicines are not usually needed; your team can prescribe symptom relief if required.

support.title: Immune alert card
support.text: Carry your alert card during treatment and afterwards. Show it when seeking urgent care; symptoms can be mistaken for an infection or an ordinary stomach upset.

support.title: Hormones and steroids
support.text: Some immune effects need steroids or hormone replacement. Follow the prescribed plan and do not stop steroids suddenly. Ask for help if symptoms worsen or you cannot take essential medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
support.text: Discuss pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 5 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding requires a specialist decision; contact your team promptly if pregnancy occurs.

questions.q: Is my treatment for metastatic cancer or to reduce recurrence after surgery?
questions.a: Ask your team to write down the treatment aim. For metastatic disease, the aim is usually cancer control, symptom relief and more time. After complete surgery and platinum chemotherapy, adjuvant treatment aims to reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.q: Which tumour-test results support this plan?
questions.a: For the first-line metastatic monotherapy pathway, the source requires high PD-L1 expression and no EGFR mutation or ALK translocation. The adjuvant pathway has different eligibility. Ask which results apply to your own cancer.

questions.q: How long is my course, and what could change it?
questions.a: Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.

questions.q: Who arranges blood and thyroid tests between visits?
questions.a: The oncology team arranges and reviews tests. Blood count, kidney/liver function and glucose are checked before each cycle; thyroid tests are usually every 3–6 weeks. Ask whether an extra test is needed between treatment visits.

questions.q: Which symptoms should I report straight away, and whom do I contact out of hours?
questions.a: Report new or worsening breathing problems, persistent diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, yellow eyes, reduced urine, severe headache, weakness, thirst or a spreading rash promptly. Keep the local oncology and out-of-hours numbers available; severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain needs 112 / 999.

questions.q: What are my alternatives if I choose not to have this treatment?
questions.a: Ask about alternatives for your exact stage and tumour results, including other anticancer treatments, trials, surveillance where appropriate and symptom-focused care. Supportive care remains available whether or not you proceed.

sections.title: Appointments
sections.text: Atezolizumab 1200 mg is given by intravenous infusion on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The first infusion lasts about 60 minutes; later infusions may last 30 minutes if tolerated. The visit includes checks and preparation. This protocol also offers a separately prescribed 1875 mg injection under the skin of the thigh over about 7 minutes every 3 weeks. The IV and under-skin doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

sections.title: Course length
sections.text: Adjuvant treatment lasts up to 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance continue until progression or unacceptable toxicity, with regular individual review.

sections.title: Checks between visits
sections.text: Blood tests are due before each infusion. Thyroid tests stay every 3–6 weeks regardless of dose schedule. Ask about travel, work, transport and whom to contact if a test or visit is delayed.

sections.title: Home medicines and records
sections.text: Keep the alert card, symptom record, current medicine list and urgent contact details accessible. Your team may prescribe steroids or hormone replacement only if needed.

sections.title: After the final dose
sections.text: Keep reporting new symptoms. Some hormone medicines and monitoring continue after the cancer treatment finishes.

anatomy: Severe headache, confusion, weakness, dizziness or marked thirst need prompt advice.
New cough or breathlessness can signal inflammation or another urgent cause.
Chest pain, racing heartbeat or fainting needs urgent assessment.
Yellow eyes/skin or dark urine may signal inflammation; tests also check the liver.
Report much less urine, new swelling or a change in kidney tests.
New or persistent diarrhoea, blood in stools or severe tummy pain needs urgent advice.
Spreading rash, blisters, severe weakness or muscle pain needs prompt review.

scope_note: Lung settings: previously treated NSCLC; first-line PD-L1-high metastatic NSCLC; adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy; ES-SCLC maintenance after induction. Urothelial uses in the shared clinical protocol require their own patient discussion.

evidence.title: Why this treatment may be offered
evidence.intro: Atezolizumab may help the immune system control suitable lung cancers. After surgery and chemotherapy, it can reduce recurrence risk in a selected group. In small-cell cancer it continues an induction-plus-maintenance treatment plan. These settings have different evidence and aims; trial results cannot predict one person’s outcome.
evidence.interpretation: Separate lung settings and trials; group results are not personal predictions.
evidence.population: Lung settings: previously treated NSCLC; first-line PD-L1-high metastatic NSCLC; adjuvant NSCLC after surgery and platinum chemotherapy; ES-SCLC maintenance after induction.
evidence.limitations: OAK, IMpower110, IMpower010 and IMpower133 used 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks. The 840 mg every 2 weeks, 1680 mg every 4 weeks and SC schedules rely on pharmacokinetic/formulation bridging, not separate head-to-head efficacy trials.

items.title: Other options
items.text: Discuss other systemic treatments, targeted therapy when appropriate, clinical trials, surveillance and symptom-focused care with your team.

items.title: PD-L1 blockade
items.text: Atezolizumab blocks PD-L1, a protein that can help cancer cells evade immune attack. Blocking PD-L1 can help immune cells attack cancer, but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs.

items.title: Healthy organs can be affected
items.text: Immune inflammation can affect lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys, skin, glands, muscles, heart and nerves. It may need steroids, hospital care or long-term hormone replacement, and can start after treatment ends.

chapters.title: Your treatment course
chapters.intro: Appointments and total course length are separate decisions.

items.title: Administration
items.text: Atezolizumab 1200 mg is given by intravenous infusion on Day 1 every 3 weeks (21 days). The first infusion lasts about 60 minutes; later infusions may last 30 minutes if tolerated. The visit includes checks and preparation. This protocol also offers a separately prescribed 1875 mg injection under the skin of the thigh over about 7 minutes every 3 weeks. The IV and under-skin doses are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.

items.title: Course length
items.text: Adjuvant: maximum 12 months. Advanced NSCLC and ES-SCLC maintenance: until progression or unacceptable toxicity. ES-SCLC requires completed induction; this suite contains no induction chemotherapy.

items.title: Pauses and changes
items.text: Your team may withhold or stop treatment for side effects. Atezolizumab is not routinely dose-reduced. Tell the team about a missed appointment; do not assume the old appointment schedule still applies.

chapters.title: Tests and review
chapters.intro: Normal recent tests do not exclude new immune symptoms.

items.title: Before starting
items.text: Confirm diagnosis, treatment setting and relevant biomarkers. Blood count, kidney/liver profile, glucose, thyroid and hepatitis screening provide a baseline. Discuss existing illness and all medicines.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 3-week treatment cycle; thyroid every 3–6 weeks; other hormones when clinically indicated. Symptoms need review during and after treatment.

items.title: After stopping
items.text: Continue agreed symptom, hormone and scan follow-up. Keep your immune alert card and urgent contact details.

chapters.title: Practical support and everyday life
chapters.intro: Keep your team informed about what matters to you.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Fatigue can affect daily activities. Balance activity with rest and ask for help if tiredness is new, marked or accompanied by dizziness, headache, thirst or weakness; it may need medical assessment.

items.title: Eating, drinking and bowels
items.text: Drink as advised and report ongoing vomiting or diarrhoea. Do not assume diarrhoea is a minor stomach upset; your team needs to check for immune inflammation and other causes.

items.title: Medicines and pregnancy
items.text: Bring a full medicine list, including supplements and steroids. Ask before starting new medicines. Use the contraception plan and discuss fertility or breastfeeding with your team.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Use the contact plan given by your oncology service.

items.title: Report warning symptoms
items.text: Contact the oncology team immediately for new or worsening breathlessness, chest pain, persistent diarrhoea, severe tummy pain, yellow skin/eyes, much less urine, severe headache, marked weakness, confusion, unusual thirst or passing much more urine, or a spreading/blistering rash. For severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or other immediately dangerous symptoms, seek emergency care. Do not wait for the next infusion.

items.title: During the drip
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately if you become itchy, flushed, breathless, dizzy, tight-chested or suddenly unwell.

items.title: Care after treatment ends
items.text: Immune inflammation can start late. Tell any healthcare team about atezolizumab even after the course has finished.
